articles.title: Pope Leo gets rapturous welcome on return to Peru: ‘This visit is like a big party’
articles.summary: Pontiff is visiting the country, where he spent nearly a decade as bishop, during an 11-day South American tour
body: The walls in Chiclayo have been painted with colourful murals and banners welcoming Pope Leo XIV, but he is better known to residents of this city in northern Peru as “Padre Roberto” – a pastor who walked their streets, shared their love of local cuisine, and stood by them through natural disasters and the Covid-19 pandemic.
Robert Prevost, 71, who spent nearly a decade as the bishop here until he left in 2023, has returned to his former home as the Catholic church’s most powerful figure.
As many as a million people were expected to turn out for Leo’s first big mass in Peru, due to be held in a field outside the coastal city on Friday.
Yet for the city’s faithful he remains humble and approachable, the characteristics that first endeared him to them.

Prevost is not only the first pope from the United States, he is also the first to hold citizenship in Peru, and he has set aside six days to visit it on the final leg of an 11-day South American trip that passed through Uruguay and Argentina.

Prevost, though born in Chicago, has been coming and going from Peru for four decades, spending about 20 years of his pastoral life in his fervently Catholic adopted nation beginning in 1985, when the 29-year-old Augustinian missionary arrived in Chulucanas, a poor town in the far north of the country.

To say Peruvians are delighted at his return visit as pope is an understatement. Tens of thousands lined the streets of Lima as Leo’s cavalcade drove him from the airport to the presidential palace on Wednesday. After Chiclayo, he travels to the Andean town of Santa Cruz; the African-Peruvian town of Zaña; Cusco, the one-time Inca capital; and Pucallpa, a city in the Peruvian Amazon, before returning to Lima.
“This visit is like a big party,” said José Luis Pérez Guadalupe, a theologian and professor at Lima’s Pacific University. “Peruvians want to celebrate their first ever pope.”

It seems clear that for Pope Leo, it is an emotional reunion, too. When he made his inaugural speech from the balcony overlooking St Peter’s Square in May 2025, he switched from Italian to Spanish in order to mention his former diocese in Chiclayo.

“He was a man of action, not just words,” recalls Yolanda Díaz, 72, who worked closely with Prevost in the Chiclayo diocese. “It was really hard to see him just sitting down. He was always walking around with his shoes covered in dust.”

He is particularly remembered for his work during the Covid-19 pandemic. He did not just deliver food aid, but gave last rites to victims – of which Peru had some of the highest figures per capita, with more than 219,000 deaths – at a time when funeral gatherings were banned due to the perceived risk of contagion. When victims were dying in the streets and even in hospitals due to a lack of oxygen, he raised $380,000 through the Catholic charity Caritas to buy two oxygen plants.

“When aid needed to be delivered to remote areas, he would be in the helicopter, taking it himself. He wasn’t just giving orders,” Díaz said. “He would always talk to you face-to-face, never from behind a desk or a pulpit. He knew how to listen, discuss and then resolve any issue.”

Prevost appointed Díaz to lead the diocese’s commission on human mobility and human trafficking to deal with the influx of destitute migrant families, many of whom had walked and hitchhiked from Venezuela in 2018 at the height of that country’s hyperinflation crisis. About 20,000 passed through Chiclayo, and 3,500 families settled in the region, according to the commission. Peru received 1.6 million migrants, the second-highest number after Colombia. Overall, about 7 million Venezuelans, a third of the population, have migrated mostly within Latin America.

Díaz led efforts to establish Venezuelans’ legal status so they could work, access housing and schooling for their children. Some Venezuelans joined the commission, too, including Lisbeth Díaz, a schoolteacher who arrived in Chiclayo in August 2018 with two children. She helped to organise soup kitchens that Prevost promoted to assist migrants and combat human trafficking.

“Without the church we would have been lost, but we had such great support,” she said. “To me, he was – and continues to be – a person who radiates great peace and serenity. He is a very peaceful person, deeply committed to those most in need, to the poor.”
Pope Leo met six victims of clerical abuse, amid criticism that his public agenda was manipulated by conservative sectors of the church in Peru to avoid such potentially uncomfortable encounters.

Leo spent over an hour with the victims, meeting “each person individually, listening to their stories of suffering and their pain”, and “thanked them for their invaluable testimony”, the Vatican said.

Together, “they reflected on how to foster a shift in mindset – by listening to victims, seeking the truth, pursuing paths toward healing, and committing to the creation of safe environments”, it said.

Last week, Bishop Accountability, a US-based NGO, published a list of 77 Peruvian priests, brothers and lay members accused of sexual abuse and pederasty, as part of its global database. Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, dissolved the Peru-based Catholic movement Sodalitium over its abuses in 2025, but elements linked to the powerful organisation continue to harass the journalists behind the investigation that led to its downfall.

Camila Bustamante, a Chilean journalist who published a book denouncing abuses in a female arm of Sodalitium, said she was surprised to receive an invitation to meet Pope Leo in Lima. “I hope he listens and takes this information and does something with it,” she said.

Silvia Alayo, who worked with Prevost at Peru’s Episcopal Commission on Social Action, said she was disappointed such meetings had not been made priorities but she believed Leo would follow the example of the late Pope Francis with a “no tolerance” stance on abuse.
“I believe in his commitment to truth and justice,” she added, insisting that victims must receive reparations from the church.

In an address to bishops earlier on Thursday, Leo described the “pain” caused by Catholic clerical abuse and said the church must make “amends” to victims and foster “a culture of prevention and protection”.
Related: Pope Leo delivers stinging rebuke of Milei’s austerity measures during Argentina visit
Clerical abuse was “a reality that has caused us so much pain”, the 71-year-old said.

The pope’s more immediate concern may be getting through his gruelling schedule following an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung after a cancer diagnosis a month ago. Doctors have since given him the all clear.

“In the past, there was an unwritten rule that there would never be a pope from the US due to its dominant hegemonic power,” said Pérez Guadalupe. But Prevost’s “talent for listening and dialogue” helped the conclave not see Prevost as just a US candidate, but also a Latin American pontiff. “Peru made Pope Leo who he is. Now he has returned to his roots.”

articles.title: Banned books from Ireland’s room of ‘evil literature’ finally see the light of day
articles.summary: Censored books spanning 1926-96 contained themes ‘likely to corrupt or deprave’, or references to contraception or violence
body: For almost a century, an Irish government building in the heart of Dublin has hosted a secret sanctum: the banned books room.
The department of justice, on St Stephen’s Green, did not grant public access, because the shelves contained 12,000 books deemed indecent or obscene.
It was a graveyard for titles condemned by the Censorship of Publications Board, a guardian of public morals which guillotined anything that smelled of sex or other corruptions.
Harold Robbins was interred. So too Ian Fleming, Edna O’Brien, Brendan Behan, Oscar Wilde, DH Lawrence, JD Salinger, John Updike, Iris Murdoch, F Scott Fitzgerald and many more.

Exhumation, however, is nigh. The entire collection is to be moved to the National Archives as part of the repeal of Ireland’s censorship laws. The censors’ notes, minutes and ledgers that detail why each book was banned will be made publicly available for the first time – a trove for researchers of social history and state control.

“The censors prohibited works that they saw as contravening or subverting public morality – anything that was seen as unwholesome or suggestive of sexual immorality,” said Orlaith McBride, the director of the National Archives. “It was often just the innuendo of something that could have been perceived as likely to corrupt or deprave.”
The volumes span 1926 to 1996 and encompass pulp fiction, high-brow literature and academic texts. References to family planning, contraception and violence were likely to elicit bans, said McBride.

So too did suggestive imagery, such as the cover of O’Brien’s groundbreaking 1960 novel, The Country Girls. “It’s very subtly done but you can see the contours of the female form. The issue wasn’t just the contents but the image,” McBride said.

Banned titles included classics such as Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Gray, Behan’s Borstal Boy and Lawrence’s Lady Chatterley’s Lover, as well as pulpy paperbacks with titles such as The Baby Doll Murders, A Doctor and his Mistress and Torrid Tale of a Wicked Town.

Scholarly tomes such as Sexual Life in England Past and Present and arcane works such as The Collected Works of Pierre Louÿs, a Belgian poet of the early 20th century, also ended up in what was informally called the banned books room.
The censorship board adopted a broad definition of indecent and obscene, said Brian Hughes, a history lecturer at the University of Limerick’s Mary Immaculate College.

“I think people would be very surprised seeing these books or reading some of these books to think that they were banned at all in the first place, because attitudes are quite different now. I think it suggests that certainly in terms of printed matter, the written word, there’s a much more liberal society. It is a more secular society as well; that’s part of it. But I think it’s a wider process of attitudes towards sex, sexuality changing.”

In 1926, soon after independence, the nascent Irish Free State established the Committee of Evil Literature, a five-man panel tasked with protecting public morals. It recommended a strict system of vetting that led to the Censorship of Publications Board – which, for a time, was led by a Catholic priest – and an appeals board.
The censors reviewed material that was submitted by members of the public and customs and revenue officers. They also sourced books through a subscription to the Times Book Club.

The periodicals and books that accumulated at what is now known as the department of justice, home affairs and migration will be moved after Christmas to the National Archives, where they will be conserved, catalogued and stored.

“Many are first editions, and because of sheer age in a vulnerable state, so they won’t be available to the public,” said McBride. People could source them online “and in all good bookshops”, she said.

The censors’ registers and notes, plus letters from the public and interest groups, were transferred this week, and are undergoing conservation in advance of becoming publicly available. McBride said: “They are the most interesting because they record the decisions and reveal the thinking behind the bans.”

articles.title: Iran says it targeted US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
articles.summary: First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower
body: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months.

“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”
US Central Command denied that the radar system had been destroyed and said US forces had intercepted two Iranian drones headed for Bahrain.

Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Trump said he had asked the vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.

Vance has been at the forefront of Republicans saying the war was the cause of the widespread Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public because higher diesel prices were a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

An opinion poll in the UK showed 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu).
It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was 45%, with 22% opposed.

The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda.

Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.”

Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon.

In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for a review of Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”.

The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning.

Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely in political and security circles.
Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested.

The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

articles.title: Moscow car bomb severely injures former aide to Ukraine’s pro-Russia ex-PM
articles.summary: Attack thought to be orchestrated by Kyiv comes day after Russian military official was killed in blast in St Petersburg
body: Russia has been rocked by two car bomb attacks that killed a senior military figure and seriously injured a suspected intelligence agent, in the latest in a series of assassination attempts believed to have been orchestrated by Kyiv.
On Friday morning a car bomb exploded in southern Moscow, severely injuring Sergei Zavorotniy, 72, a former senior aide to Ukraine’s exiled former prime minister Mykola Azarov.
Russian media reported that Zavorotniy was in an induced coma after losing his left arm in the blast, which also gave him concussion, fractured ribs and other injuries.
Russia’s Investigative Committee said it had launched a criminal investigation into the explosion.
Zavorotniy served as a spokesperson and adviser to Azarov, who fled to Russia in 2014 after Ukraine’s Maidan revolution toppled the pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych.

A 2020 report by the US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence investigating Russian interference in the 2016 US presidential election identified Zavorotniy as an officer of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) involved in influence operations.
The blast in Russia’s capital came a day after a car bomb explosion in St Petersburg killed a senior Russian military official.
That explosion occurred on Thursday morning in the city’s Pushkinsky district, an area home to many military personnel, according to law enforcement officials and media reports.
The victim, who has not been publicly identified, was a colonel in the Russian air force, according to sources cited by the local broadcaster 78.ru.
Fontanka, a St Petersburg-based news outlet, reported that the colonel was killed by a remotely detonated bomb planted by a 31-year-old suspect.
According to the outlet, the suspect had tracked the colonel’s movements for months after securing a job at a nearby shop. He reportedly fled Russia for Moldova via Turkey on Thursday morning.
Ukraine has not yet commented on the two attacks.

Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have targeted dozens of senior Russian military officers and Russia-installed officials whom it accuses of involvement in war crimes.

The latest two attacks, carried out in the heavily policed cities of Moscow and St Petersburg, highlight the continued struggle of Russia’s security services to protect senior military personnel nearly five years into the war. In late August a lieutenant colonel serving in a Russian air force and air defence unit was killed in a car bombing in the same St Petersburg neighbourhood.
Vladimir Putin has previously reprimanded his top security officials over the wave of assassinations, prompting tighter security measures.

Little is known about the clandestine Ukrainian networks believed to be operating inside Russia and Russian-occupied territories, carrying out assassinations and attacks on military infrastructure far behind the frontlines.

articles.title: Russia strikes hospital in central Kyiv after SpaceX system falters again
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says speed restrictions on Starshield system made it harder for Ukraine to shoot down drones
body: Russia has attacked a hospital in the centre of Kyiv, close to several western embassies, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said speed restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield system had made it harder for Ukraine to shoot down enemy drones.
Three people were injured when a drone smashed into the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics at 3am, hitting the second floor of the hospital and an adjoining 19th-century building.

Meanwhile, Russia claimed it had shot down nearly 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight, one of the largest swarms sent by Kyiv. It reported that at least four people were killed in the southern region of Volgograd.

The blast in Kyiv blew out windows in nearby buildings including in the National Academy of Arts across the road. The six-storey hospital is located in the Shevchenkivskyi district, not far from the Danish and Romanian embassies, as well as cafes and a park popular with dog walkers.

Standing in the yard as smoke billowed from the burning building, and firefighters led dazed patients to safety, one witness, Oleksandr, said the attack had narrowly missed patients. “We were asleep when there was this massive boom. We all jumped out of bed straight away.
“There was glass all over the floor. People were running about … If it had hit a little further to the left it would have been much worse. We felt the shock wave.”

He added: “Targeting the wounded – that’s really low. Russia attacks everything. Where I live, high-rise blocks are being constantly hit by bombs. They don’t care where they drop them, or where they land.”

Russia has recently stepped up its strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, hitting power plants, passenger trains and two bridges across the Dnipro river. Ukraine says the attacks are part of a campaign of terror, designed to make a weary population capitulate.

On Thursday, Zelenskyy said the Starshield system – operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and overseen by the Pentagon – was again experiencing significant disruptions, after an unexplained slowdown last month.

He said some Russian aerial sorties had got through because Ukrainian interceptor systems that rely on the US satellite service could not reach the necessary speed to knock out enemy drones. Starshield is the Ukrainian military’s version of Starlink.

The White House has yet to explain why the service has been throttled for a second time, but it comes after intense US-led shuttle diplomacy this week, with Donald Trump seemingly pressuring Zelenskyy to make territorial concessions to Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.

Trump’s emissaries, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real estate developer Steve Witkoff, met Putin in Moscow on Thursday. They then flew to Dublin to brief Zelenskyy on their talks, which came after trilateral negotiations on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi.

Kremlin negotiators insist that Ukraine hand over four Ukrainian provinces, including cities and villages Russian troops have been unable to conquer. They are also calling for a new “security architecture” in Europe – a demand in effect that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture, before eastern European nations joined the alliance.

At the same time, Moscow does not want European states to be involved in US-brokered talks to end the war in Ukraine. On Thursday, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, said Europe had to take part since “US support” for Kyiv had ended.
“Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” Macron said. “At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”

Meanwhile, Russian strikes ⁠on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ⁠overnight caused ⁠power ​outages in 12 ⁠regions, said deputy energy minister Artem ⁠Nekrasov. The ‌affected regions are ‌Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Zhytomyr, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Rivne, Sumy, Kharkiv, ‌Khmelnytskyi and Chernihiv.
“Energy workers ​are working at an intensified pace, ⁠but new attacks ​and constant ​air raid ​alerts ​are ‌complicating and delaying ​repairs,” ​Nekrasov said.
In Kyiv, the orthopaedic hospital’s director, Roman Derkach, said medical services had been temporarily suspended as a cleanup operation got under way. Thirty patients were taken to safety.

articles.title: Friday briefing: Why people are turning to folklore in our disconnected age
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: ​Old and new rituals still resonate in today’s folk revival which is being shaped by younger generations seeking spirituality, community and connection to nature
body: Good morning. What are your plans for this Friday 13th? Will you be edging your way through the day, alert to impending disasters and saluting every magpie you see (a cheerful “good day, captain” works for me). Or will you be powering past the superstition with the insouciance that accompanies the certainty this is, probably, just another day?

Either way, I’ve noticed that folklore – the rituals, traditions and stories we share together – is enjoying a significant revival across our pop culture and community practice, powered by the younger generation and accelerated by online connections.
This explosion in engagement is the opposite of dusty nostalgia but instead focused on very contemporary concerns about connection with both the Earth and each other.

For today’s newsletter, as a major survey charting contemporary folk culture in England comes to an end next month, I spoke to three folklore experts about why these customs still matter. First, this morning’s headlines.

Technology | Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams and other apps were disrupted for thousands of users for more than nine hours, with Microsoft scrambling to find a solution after initial fixes failed to bring services back online.

US news | Nvidia’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s commerce secretary are expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks, as the fallout from Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy sparked bipartisan concerns for national security and calls for a tougher stance against Beijing.

UK news | Young people with disabilities will lose their personal independence payments and will have to apply to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment, Alan Milburn’s review will recommend.
UK politics | Nigel Farage appeared on Russell Brand’s US podcast nine months after the comedian was investigated by police over allegations of sexual assault, the Guardian has learned.
Climate crisis | China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

It’s been hard to miss the wave of representations of folkloric tales and practice in popular media in recent years – think folk horror movies like Hereditary, Midsommar and The Ritual on the big screen, or The League of Gentlemen, the Detectorists and Small Prophets on the small screen.

This has been accompanied by thriving online folk communities, many aimed at gen Z, exploring urban legends, spell-making and paganism, and offline a surge in people actively participating in seasonal calendar customs. ​There’s the Mari Lwyd local to south Wales, a ghastly skeletal hobby horse who travels around people’s houses in midwinter with a group of wassailers to scare and entertain, and Whuppity Scoorie, a children’s spring festival in Lanark, first documented in the 1890s. And with renewed interest comes an expanded community: Jack in the Green, the annual May Day skirmish in Hastings, has included a LGBTQI+ troupe for 30 years.

Folklorists tracking this revival wanted to learn more, resulting in the National Folklore Survey for England, coordinated by the Centre for Contemporary Legend at Sheffield Hallam University. An ambitious two-year undertaking, which draws to a close in December, it is based around a snapshot study of almost 2,000 participants and provides the most comprehensive picture of contemporary folk culture in England to date.

Dr Diane A Rodgers, the project co-lead, and researcher Dr Sophie Parkes-Nield are still collating their embarrassment of data, but some fascinating trends have already emerged. These include the prevalence of beliefs (one-third of respondents believe that ghosts exist) and that younger age-groups were twice as likely to believe in conspiracy theories, demons and curses as older respondents. There’s also the intergenerational reach of contemporary legends: nearly half of 16- to 24-year-olds believe that Diana, Princess of Wales was murdered as a result of a conspiracy, despite not being born when she died in 1997.
The results also reveal how folkloric practice is woven into everyday life. I’m not alone in my acknowledgment of magpies: 51% do something similar, whether that’s saluting, speaking or spitting.

“Do you say something when you see a magpie? Do you pick a penny off the pavement? Do you touch wood when you want something to happen?” Rodgers asks me. Absolutely everyone has folklore, she believes, and we see it in small ways every single day: “whether it’s the Christmas pudding recipe annotated by your great-grandma that you make every year, or pupils signing each other’s shirts at the end of the school term”.

A lot of us don’t realise we’re participating in folklore, says Parkes-Nield. “If you blow out candles on a birthday cake, if you take part in the ritualised behaviour involved in a stag or hen do, all of those things are folkloric”.

In essence, folklore is the practices, traditions and stories people share together. It encompasses crafts, dance, songs, tales, beliefs. And it usually has an element of received knowledge passed from one generation to the next, and that evolves by word of mouth rather than formalised means.

Folklore is sometimes best explained by what it’s not: not purely historical, not only the paranormal, not just middle-aged white men morris dancing around isolated villages where incomers face ritual immolation.

Indeed, morris dancing is a fine example of the more inclusive aspect of the folk revival: once exclusively male, there are now as many female dancers as men, with the growth of queer and feminist troupes like Boss Morris, who have performed with Wet Leg at the Brit Awards and Glastonbury.
Why are younger people so engaged in folklore?

Folklore can be very analogue, says Parkes-Nield. It’s tangible and, particularly in a post-pandemic world, a way to meet the people on your doorstep – whether it is learning a heritage craft like wheat-weaving, editing a fanzine or visiting local standing stones with other curious neighbours.

And, while folklore absolutely proliferates through digital means – look up WitchTok or #pagan on your social media of choice – it also offers a way of getting offline and meeting people across generations, in a time when so much entertainment is segregated and screen-based.

All of this has pretty obvious positive effects for mental health, as young people in particular struggle in an increasingly disconnected world. And it satisfies a craving for spiritual exploration that extends beyond organised religion – according to recent census data shamanism is the fastest growing belief system in the UK.

In her research, Parkes-Nield sees folklore societies popping up all over the shop – one such is Folk Club, based in south London and set up four years ago by Ellie Dempsey and Elizabeth Bailey. Now in her early 30s, Bailey grew up in the countryside, but didn’t really consider the folk rituals that were part of her childhood until she moved to the capital.

The escalating climate emergency is without doubt tied to the current resurgence, she thinks. “Folklore often sees a revival at points of national crisis, because it’s so much about coming together and connecting with the natural world.”

But, while Bailey also notes an appetite for learning about the seasonal traditions that were once passed down organically, the pull is not backwards. “A big part of the folk revival is that folk is by the people, for the people. That means re-examining some practices, making them more inclusive, and taking the opportunity to update traditions that have stagnated or been co-opted.”

She also draws a direct line between the political roots of folklore and this current iteration, like the Right to Roam protesters summoning Old Crockern, the mythical guardian spirit of Dartmoor, or Extinction Rebellion crowds banging pots and pans. “This is folklore being created.”

The folklore revival has been greeted with scepticism in some quarters, wary of the potential for co-option for a more nationalist or far-right agenda. The academics and practitioners I spoke to are well aware of how “Englishness” has become contentious in recent years, in particular the aggressive use of the St George’s flag by anti-immigrant activists.

But they argue these customs are far from nationalistic – many happen on a more hyperlocal scale than national. Folklore is often historically anti-establishment, and its practices at times suppressed with the same force and misogyny directed towards women accused of witchcraft. There are plenty of calendar customs, for example, cancelled by the establishment because of what was considered to be riotous behaviour by the lower classes. And many traditions were founded by communities wanting to celebrate themselves beyond the dominant culture: the Notting Hill carnival is perhaps the best-known example of this.

Academics talk about “multifolkloric Britain”, says Rodgers. “We can’t track where certain elements of folklore come from because we’ve always had people arriving and leaving, bringing and taking away things. So folklore is naturally diverse and inclusive.”
But the current revival is offering a moment of correction. She quotes the writer David Southwell, creator of the folkloric fantasy Hookland, who argues: “Re-enchantment is resistance”.

Our critics’ roundup of the best things to watch, read, play and listen to right now

MusicBlackhaine: Saints in the Wethouse | ★★★★☆His Playboi Carti collabs may have dragged Tom Heyes out of the underground, but this bracing debut remains far from the mainstream, full of garbled barks and walls of noise. Read Alexis Petridis’s full review.

TVMums v Big Pharma (BBC iPlayer) | ★★★★☆Janet Williams and Emma Murphy both had children with disabilities, then started doing some digging and uncovered a jaw-dropping medical fiasco that rivals thalidomide. Read Lucy Mangan’s full review.

GameTanuki: Pon’s Summer | ★★★★☆This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration. Read Christian Donlan’s full review.
“Nvidia chief quits after claims of affairs with ‘spy’ and employee”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while the FT goes with “Huang exit plunges Nvidia into crisis”.
The Times leads on “Six women say they too were preyed on by Brand”, the Sun writes “Monster’s mansion”.

The i Paper has “Britain set for a new deal with the EU”, the Mail’s take is “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset”, and the Express says “PM’ ‘obsessed with selling us out to the EU’”. The Telegraph says “Taxman to hound bereaved for decades”, the Mirror has “100 knives off our streets every day”, and Metro writes “Not so flush now”.
Why Democrat Scott Colom’s victory in Mississippi Senate race was so historic

Mississippi has elected the Democrat Scott Colom in a historic race in the traditionally deep-red state, making him its first Black senator since shortly after the US civil war. The closely contested race was called more than a week after the US midterms, with Colom running against the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith. How did Colom’s grassroots campaign win despite limited early backing from national Democrats? Lucy Hough speaks to politics and democracy reporter George Chidi.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Datacentres are usually built without the consent of locals, consume vast amounts of electricity and water, and enrich rapacious tech companies.

But in Falun, Sweden, stands a datacentre with a difference. Made from wood, its electricity supply is 100% renewable, its back-up generators run on a fossil-free biofuel, and it pumps its excess heat into Falun’s local district heating system. These are just a few of its sustainable credentials.
Its creation was also initiated by government with local benefits built in, such as 60% of its capital expenditure being invested locally in areas such as education, training and youth activities.
Datacentres may be an inevitable part of our digital future, but Sweden’s approach shows there might be a kinder way to get there.

articles.title: More than 60% of Germany’s female soldiers report harassment or abuse
articles.summary: Defence minister says extent of sexual misconduct found by study is ‘unacceptable’, as military tries to attract more recruits
body: Germany’s defence minister has promised a “zero tolerance” approach to sexual abuse in the armed forces after a study found soldiers, particularly women, faced extensive harassment within the ranks.

The first comprehensive study of its kind into the Bundeswehr, conducted by the Centre for Military History and Social Sciences in Potsdam and released this week, comes as the military is trying to attract new recruits in response to global threats.

It found that more than 60% of female soldiers had reported experiencing some form of sexual harassment or abuse while on duty, ranging from sexually explicit remarks and degrading rituals to sexual violence.

Nearly 40% of the 4,000 women who responded to the survey said they had been addressed with suggestive comments and sexualised remarks, while 15% reported being harassed with mobile phone pictures taken against their will and in some cases altered using AI.
Just over 8% reported having been physically attacked, and 2% said they had been the victims of sexual violence.
Around 19% of male ‌soldiers had experienced a similar form of sexual misconduct, with non-binary or gay soldiers disproportionately affected, the study found.

Boris Pistorius, the defence minister, said the figures were “unacceptable”, in particular for a military that is trying to considerably increase its numbers. The Bundeswehr has pumped billions into boosting both personnel and equipment. Military bosses have set a target of 260,000 active-duty troops and 200,000 reservists by 2035, in the hope of avoiding the introduction of conscription.

Pistorius said he was struck by the finding that women in units with a higher proportion of other women were less frequently affected, which he said “argues in favour of recruiting more women into the Bundeswehr”.

He said he had been advised by some colleagues to ditch the study, over fears it would sully the reputation of the military. To do so, he said, would be akin to “turning a blind eye”, which in the long term would do more damage to the Bundeswehr. The study would be repeated every year, he added.
“Zero tolerance applies to sexual harassment within the Bundeswehr,” the minister said.

Pistorius expressed concern over a high level of reluctance to report incidents. About a third of those surveyed said they did not or would not report incidents because of a lack of trust in what their superiors would do.
Before the study results were made public, Pistorius set up a hotline this month, meant to serve military personnel, which is to be staffed around the clock, and is called HELP.

In future, Pistorius said, those who made complaints should receive more information about the status of their proceedings, after victims said they were often left in the dark, but expected to continue serving.

The ministry said that, of 45,000 active or former members of the armed forces contacted to participate in the survey, 18% responded. It said its analysis showed that the figures were nevertheless representative.

articles.title: ‘The time is ripe’: ex-helicopter engineer poised to be Germany’s first female president
articles.summary: Backed by MPs from across the political divide, Bavarian Ilse Aigner offers an approachability and warmth the chancellor lacks
body: Germany has had 12 presidents since the end of the second world war, all of them men. Now, for the first time, the federal republic is on the brink of getting a female head of state. But Ilse Aigner, the lead candidate for the post, is unusual in more ways than one.
“No law degree. No marriage. No penis,” is how the left-leaning Taz newspaper put it this week – a wry, if blunt, assessment of what a break with history the 61-year-old Bavarian represents.
Friedrich Merz, Germany’s Christian Democrat (CDU) chancellor, put Aigner forward as his candidate this week after months of speculation, saying it was “high time” a woman took up the role.

If elected in January, Aigner will succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier in what is a largely ceremonial role but nonetheless Germany’s highest state position. And as she has the backing not only of Merz’s CDU but his Social Democrat partners and the opposition Greens, little is standing in her way.

Some are delighted. Jörg Thadeusz, a liberal writer and popular TV presenter with a penchant for satire, has taken his enthusiasm for Aigner so far as to have the name Ilse tattooed on his upper left arm. Pictures of him revealing the tattoo on TV this week made headline news, as media talked of the Aigner-Welle (Aigner wave) to describe the unexpected ripple of enthusiasm for the Catholic Bavarian – among the political establishment, at least.

“Ilse Aigner is … a candidate who right now could really do Germany some good,” said Thadeusz. Unlike far-right populists who were polarising the country with their demands for “Deutschland First”, he said, Aigner embraced a form of Heimat (homeland) that was “neither folklore nor a political battle cry”.

Not everyone shares his enthusiasm. Aigner’s relationship with the populist Alternative für Deutschland, the largest opposition force in the Bundestag, got off to a tricky start this week after she turned down their demand to present herself to them as a candidate. Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader and the most prominent woman in German politics, accused Aigner of failing to respect “democratic culture and manners” as well as “the millions of voters we represent”.

Despite having held a cabinet position, as agriculture minister from 2008 to 2013 under Angela Merkel, Aigner is not a household name. She began in local politics 30 years ago and entered the Bundestag in 1998. Instead of the usually prerequisite degree, she has a vocational qualification as an electrical engineer with a speciality in manufacturing helicopters, her job before entering politics.
“She’s the first head of state of the Federal Republic of Germany who can personally repair a government helicopter,” Thadeusz quipped this week.

In her nomination speech this week, Aigner said she hoped to inspire aspirational Germans: “As the first woman in the highest state office, I would stand with my person and my background as a symbol of the promise of upward mobility in our country.”

Aigner has spoken openly about surviving two serious tumour diagnoses – one in her spinal cord when she was 17, and thyroid cancer in her 40s, when she was a minister – saying they had given her perspective as a politician.

Now feted by the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to the CDU, she once struggled to be recognised. Her attempts in the early 90s, aged 27, to become mayor of her birth town, Feldkirchen-Westerham, south-east of Munich, failed because she was unmarried, which the party of arch-conservatives said was “too unclear a condition” and made her unsuitable to serve.

She still lives in Feldkirchen-Westerham, a Bavarian town of 10,000 people, where her parents ran an electronics shop. There she shares a house on a 1970s estate living under one roof with three generations of her family, including her three older sisters and their offspring. Local people refer to her affectionally as “die Ilse” (equivalent to “the Ilse”, or “our Ilse”), and describe her as being a regular attender at town celebrations. She typically cycles, “whether to the butchers and bakers, or to the opening of a new windfarm”, one resident said.

For Merz the chance to back the first female presidency is a chance to shed his reputation as a Frauenfeind (misogynist), an image that goes back in part to his decades-long rivalry with Merkel, but has been underscored to some extent by his leadership style in office. In an editorial this week, the Münchner Merkur noted that Aigner’s perceived strengths neatly complemented the chancellor’s deficiencies: “Her approach compensates for what Merz lacks: approachability, popularity, a warmth that can absorb the effects of polarisation.”

Merkel was regarded as a powerful female trailblazer not just in Germany but around the world. She was referred to at home as “Mutti” – both a term of affection and patronisingly used to describe her supposedly maternal stewardship of the country. Five years after her departure from the political stage, feminist commenters hope Aigner might prove a symbolic boost.

“The time is ripe for a woman. We have such an under-representation of women in society, in politics, in business, and it’s high time a woman held this highest office in the land. I’m very happy about that,” said Britta Hasselmann, a leading Green MP, in a podcast interview this week.

But even more important, Hasselmann emphasised, was the extent to which Aigner might draw together a country deeply divided by ideological rifts and economic tensions, where extremists are snapping at the heels of the political centre. The presidency needed someone “who can unite people, especially in such polarised times, who is empathetic, down to earth, and who tries to send a strong signal that common ground is valued in a democracy. And I believe she is capable of that,” Hasselmann said.
